runes.name: Fee
runes.gloss: f as in fear, and v as in vine
runes.note: One rune covers both f and v. At the end of a word, write ᚠᚠ if the sound is f: leaf ᛚᛁᛁᚠᚠ, leave ᛚᛁᛁᚠ.

runes.name: Thorn
runes.note: The hard th of “thing” and the soft th of “this” share one rune.

runes.name: Ride
runes.note: Only written when an r sound is actually pronounced. In British English that means before a vowel: car is ᚳᚪ, but carry is ᚳᚫᚱᛁ.

runes.name: Car
runes.note: Covers k, hard c and ck. Its own name shows the r-dropping rule: “car” is ᚳᚪ.

runes.name: Gift
runes.note: Only the hard g. The soft g of “gem” is ᚷᚻ.

runes.name: Hail
runes.note: Also does duty as the second half of ᚳᚻ, ᚷᚻ and ᛋᚻ.

runes.name: Year
runes.note: Only the consonant y. The vowel y of “happy” is ᛁ.

runes.name: Box
runes.note: Shorthand for the two sounds k+s. Only used where English spells it x — “racks” is ᚱᚫᚳᛋ, not ᚱᚫᛉ.

runes.name: Sun
runes.gloss: s as in see, and z as in zebra
runes.note: At the end of a word, write ᛋᛋ if the sound is s: cats ᚳᚫᛏᛋᛋ, dogs ᛞᛟᚷᛋ.

runes.name: Wing
runes.note: One sound, not two. Also used for the n in “think” and “thank”.

runes.name: Up
runes.gloss: the u of fun, and the vague vowel of about
runes.note: The workhorse vowel. Any unstressed, colourless vowel is ᚢ.

runes.name: Arm
runes.gloss: long ah as in arm, bath, father
runes.note: The British “ah”. It covers the bath / grass / laugh words that a Northern or American accent says with ᚫ.

runes.name: Stone
runes.note: Optional. ᛥᚩᚾ and ᛋᛏᚩᚾ are both correct.

runes.name: Queen
runes.note: Optional. ᛢᛁᛁᚾ and ᚳᚹᛁᛁᚾ are both correct.

digraphs.gloss: j as in jog, g as in gem
sh as in share, and the s of measure

punctuation.name: Double punct
punctuation.gloss: a heavier break, like a comma

punctuation.name: Cross punct
punctuation.gloss: a full stop or section break

units.title: Your first six runes
units.subtitle: ᛏ ᚾ ᛋ ᛗ ᛁ ᚫ
units.blurb: Six runes is enough for real words. Runes spell sounds, not letters.
teach: A rune stands for a **sound**, not a letter. Write what you hear.
ᛁ is the short i of *sit*. ᚫ is the short a of *hat*.
Say each word slowly and write down the sounds in order. That is the whole method.
Two of these runes are easy to muddle: ᛏ has its arms at the **top**, ᛗ has two full legs.

units.title: Building real words
units.subtitle: ᛒ ᛞ ᛚ ᚢ ᛖ
units.blurb: Five more, and most short everyday words open up.
teach: ᛖ is the short e of *bed*. ᚢ is the u of *fun*.
ᚢ is the busiest rune in the system. Any weak, colourless vowel — the *a* of *about*, the *er* of *butter* — is ᚢ.
*Tell* is ᛏᛖᛚ, not ᛏᛖᛚᛚ. You hear one l, so you write one ᛚ. Doubled letters in English spelling almost never mean a doubled sound.

units.title: More consonants, and the r rule
units.subtitle: ᚻ ᚹ ᚳ ᚱ ᛟ
units.blurb: And the first thing that will surprise you.
teach: ᚳ covers k, hard c and ck. *Cat*, *kite* and *back* all use it.
**The r rule.** In a British accent you only pronounce r before a vowel. *Red* and *very* have an r sound; *car* and *dark* do not — so you do not write ᚱ in them.
*Car* is ᚳᚪ. *Dark* is ᛞᚪᚳ. It looks strange for about ten minutes, then it looks obvious.
A quick test: say the word. If your tongue never makes an r, do not write one.

sentences.english: The cat sat on the mat.

units.title: Th, f, g, p and ng
units.subtitle: ᚦ ᚠ ᚷ ᛈ ᛝ
units.blurb: Now you can write "the" — the commonest word in English.
teach: ᚦ does both kinds of th — the hard one in *thing* and the soft one in *this*.
ᚠ does both f and v. *Fat* is ᚠᚫᛏ, *have* is ᚻᚫᚠ.
ᛝ is a single sound, the ng of *ring*. One rune, not two. It also does the n in *think* and *thank*.
*The* is ᚦᚢ. Say it out loud unstressed and you will hear the ᚢ.

sentences.english: The pen is on the desk.

units.title: Long vowels: double it
units.subtitle: ᛁᛁ ᛖᛖ ᚢᚢ ᛟᛟ ᚣᚣ
units.blurb: One rule covers every long vowel in the language.
teach: **Double a vowel rune to make it long.** ᛁ *sit* → ᛁᛁ *seed*. ᚣ *book* → ᚣᚣ *food*. ᛟ *hot* → ᛟᛟ *thought*.
ᚢ *fun* → ᚢᚢ *turn*. ᛖ *bed* → ᛖᛖ *hair*.
This is the one place where doubling means something. Everywhere else, one sound is one rune.
Remember the r rule as you go — *turn* is ᛏᚢᚢᚾ, *more* is ᛗᛟᛟ, *hair* is ᚻᛖᛖ.

sentences.english: The bird is on the roof.

units.title: The British ah
units.subtitle: ᚪ
units.blurb: One rune, and the vowel that most marks out a southern English accent.
teach: ᚪ is the long *ah* of *arm*. It has no short partner, so it is never doubled.
It covers a set of words a Northern or American speaker says with ᚫ instead: *bath*, *grass*, *laugh*, *dance*, *chance*, *ask*, *past*.
If you say *bath* to rhyme with *math*, use ᚫ instead — the system follows your accent, not a rulebook.
And again: *far* is ᚠᚪ, *hard* is ᚻᚪᛞ. No ᚱ.

sentences.english: The car is in the garden.

units.title: Sliding vowels
units.subtitle: ᛠ ᛡ ᚩ
units.blurb: The vowels that move as you say them.
teach: ᛠ is the *ay* of *day*. ᛡ is the *i* of *time*. ᚩ is the *o* of *go*.
Each of these is one sound, so one rune — even though English spells them all sorts of ways: *day*, *make*, *rain* and *they* all take ᛠ.
Say them slowly and you can hear the vowel move. That sliding is what makes them one unit rather than two.

sentences.english: I go home in the day.
My name is on the road.

units.title: Two-rune vowels
units.subtitle: ᚪᚹ ᛟᛁ ᛁᚢ
units.blurb: Three vowels that need a pair of runes.
teach: ᚪᚹ is *now*, ᛟᛁ is *boy*, ᛁᚢ is *here*.
These make sense once you say them slowly — *now* really does slide from ᚪ towards ᚹ, and *here* from ᛁ towards ᚢ.
ᛁᚢ is where words like *near*, *year* and *beer* end up once the r has gone.

sentences.english: Come down to the house now.

units.title: Ch, j and sh
units.subtitle: ᚳᚻ ᚷᚻ ᛋᚻ
units.blurb: ᚻ is the "add an h" rune.
teach: ᚳᚻ = ch, ᚷᚻ = j, ᛋᚻ = sh. In each case it is the plain consonant plus ᚻ.
ᚷᚻ also does the soft g of *age*, *large* and *bridge* — the sound is the same as j, so the spelling is.
ᛋᚻ doubles up for the middle of *measure* and *usual*, which is the same sound with the voice on.

units.title: Y and x
units.subtitle: ᛄ ᛉ
teach: ᛄ is the consonant y of *yes* and *you*. The vowel y at the end of *happy* is just ᛁ.
ᛉ is a shortcut for the ks in *box*. Only use it where English spells an x — *racks* is ᚱᚫᚳᛋ, not ᚱᚫᛉ.
That distinction is a courtesy to the reader, not a sound difference. Both are pronounced the same.

sentences.english: Yes, you can have the box.

units.title: Voiced or voiceless?
units.subtitle: ᚠᚠ and ᛋᛋ
units.blurb: How to tell leaf from leave.
teach: ᚠ is both f and v; ᛋ is both s and z. In the middle of a word, context sorts it out.
**At the end of a word, double it if the sound is voiceless.** *Leaf* is ᛚᛁᛁᚠᚠ but *leave* is ᛚᛁᛁᚠ. *Cats* is ᚳᚫᛏᛋᛋ but *dogs* is ᛞᛟᚷᛋ.
Put a finger on your throat and say "sss" then "zzz". The buzz is voicing. No buzz, double the rune.
This falls out neatly for plurals: after t, k, p and f you get s (so double); after everything else you get z (so single).

units.title: Weak syllables
units.subtitle: Everything collapses to ᚢ
units.blurb: What happens to the parts of a word you do not stress.
teach: English hurries over unstressed syllables, and the vowel in them collapses to a vague ᚢ.
*Butter* is ᛒᚢᛏᚢ. *Comma* is ᚳᛟᛗᚢ. *About* is ᚢᛒᚪᚹᛏ. Whatever the spelling suggests, you say ᚢ.
**Syllabic l and n.** *Little* is ᛚᛁᛏᚢᛚ and *bottle* is ᛒᛟᛏᚢᛚ — put ᚢ in where you hear a faint vowel before the l.
This is the rule that makes runic spelling look most unlike English. Trust your ear.

sentences.english: My mother is in the garden.

units.title: Ligatures and layout
units.subtitle: ᛥ ᛢ ᛫
units.blurb: The last two runes, and how to set out a line of text.
teach: ᛥ is ᛋ+ᛏ joined up, and ᛢ is ᚳ+ᚹ joined up. Both are optional — *stone* is ᛥᚩᚾ or ᛋᛏᚩᚾ, whichever you prefer.
Words are traditionally separated by an interpunct ᛫ rather than a space: ᛏᚣᚣ᛫ᛒᛁᛁ᛫ᛟᛟ᛫ᚾᛟᛏ᛫ᛏᚣᚣ᛫ᛒᛁᛁ.
Commas, full stops and apostrophes work exactly as they do in English. ⁊ is an optional shorthand for *and*.
You can switch the ligatures off in Settings if you would rather write everything out.

units.title: Reading without help
units.subtitle: Short sentences
units.blurb: No multiple choice. Read it, type what it says.
teach: Read the runes aloud before you try to work out the word. Sounding it out is the whole skill.
If a word looks odd, it is almost always the r rule or a doubled vowel.
Spelling does not have to be perfect — you are being marked on whether you read it right.

freeRead.english: The dog is in the garden.
I have a small house near the river.
She went to the shop for bread and milk.
My brother works in the town.
The old man sat by the fire.
There is a bird on the roof.
He gave me the book last night.

units.title: Writing without help
units.subtitle: Your turn
units.blurb: English in, runes out — from memory.
teach: Say the phrase out loud first, then write the sounds you hear.
Check yourself against three things: is every r you wrote actually pronounced? Are the long vowels doubled? Have any silent letters crept in?

freeWrite.english: the boy has a big box

units.title: A longer passage
units.subtitle: Reading at length
units.blurb: Several sentences at a time, with the English hidden until you want it.
teach: Take it a line at a time. Read aloud, then check.
You will find you stop decoding rune by rune and start recognising whole words. That is the point at which this becomes reading.

passages.title: A morning
passages.english: It was cold when I went out. The sun was low and the grass was wet. I walked down the path to the river and sat on a stone for a long time. A bird came near, looked at me, and went again.

passages.title: The house
passages.english: My grandmother had a small house at the end of the road. There was a green door and a garden with apple trees. In the summer we would sit outside and she would tell us about the old days.

units.title: Real writing
units.subtitle: Poetry and prose
units.blurb: Text written by people who were not thinking about runes.
teach: Longer words and older wording, but exactly the same system.
Notice how much shorter runic spelling often is — *thought* is four runes, *through* is four.

passages.title: Shakespeare, Hamlet
passages.english: To be, or not to be, that is the question: whether it is nobler in the mind to suffer the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, or to take arms against a sea of troubles.

passages.title: Emma Lazarus, The New Colossus
passages.english: Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free, the wretched refuse of your teeming shore.

passages.title: The opening of Beowulf, in modern English
passages.english: Listen. We have heard of the glory of the kings of the Danes in the old days, and how those princes did brave deeds.

units.title: Everything at once
units.subtitle: The final round
units.blurb: A mixed test drawing on all thirty runes and every rule.
teach: This pulls from everything you have done. If something has slipped, the Practice tab will keep bringing it back.
After this, the most useful thing you can do is write something of your own — a note, a list, a diary line a day.

units.title: Counting in Futhorc
units.subtitle: ᚪᚾ ᛏᚹᚪ ᚦᚱᛁᛖ ᚠᛖᚩᚹᛖᚱ
units.blurb: Learn how to read and write Anglo-Saxon spelled numbers 1 to 10 in runes.
teach: Anglo-Saxons wrote numbers as spelled phonetic words rather than modern digits.
1 is *ān* (ᚪᚾ), 2 is *twā* (ᛏᚹᚪ), 3 is *þrīe* (ᚦᚱᛁᛖ), 4 is *feōwer* (ᚠᛖᚩᚹᛖᚱ), and 5 is *fīf* (ᚠᛁᚠ).
6 is *six* (ᛋᛁᚳᛋ), 7 is *seofon* (ᛋᛖᚩᚠᚩᚾ), 8 is *eahta* (ᛠᚻᛏᚪ), 9 is *nigon* (ᚾᛁᚷᚩᚾ), and 10 is *tīen* (ᛏᛁᛖᚾ).
When you enter numbers (like 42 or 1995), the app automatically spells them out using these historical Old English rules.

freeRead.english: one bird sat on a tree
i have two eyes and two hands
three green apples on the table
five red roses in the garden
